SAM11-01.note: f(1)=0, f(5)=40, (40-0)/4=10. Distractors 40 (=f(5), forgot to divide) and 8 (=f'(2)? weak) are fine. Routine average-rate-of-change; module 1 / easy end of module 2.

SAM11-02.note: w(60-2w)=400 -> w=10 or w=20. w=20 gives L=20, not longer than w, so the stated condition genuinely eliminates it. This is one of only two items where a restriction does real work. Distractor 40 is L, 20 the rejected root.

SAM11-03.note: (2x-3)^3 = 8x^3-36x^2+54x-27. Distractor 54 is the x coefficient, 36 a sign error. Near-duplicate mechanism with SAM11-14 (expand a product, extract one coefficient).

SAM11-04.note: u=sqrt(x): u=2,3 -> x=4,9, both check, sum 13. STEM ECHO, and the batch's worst case: TWO of the four options (5 and 6) are literals printed in the stem, and a third (9) is one of the two solutions. They sit on real error paths (5 = sum of the u-roots by Vieta, 6 = their product), so I agree they are not naive echoes - but a blind solver who distrusts stem literals is down to 13 vs 9 in one step. Medium on the live scale.

SAM11-05.note: min f = -4 at x=3, so max g = 4+7 = 11. Distractor 4 = -min f (forgot +7), 3 = the vertex x. Same mechanism as SAM11-17 (maximum of a downward parabola).

SAM11-06.note: (x-3)^2(x-r), product of roots 9r = -18 -> r = -2; p(x)=x^3-4x^2-3x+18, a=-4, b=-3. Distractor -3 is b (the other constant the same work produces) - strong and fair. Option 2 echoes the multiplicity 2 printed in the stem but is also |r|, a real path; I agree it is not a usable elimination. Genuinely module-2 hard.

SAM11-07.note: (3-x)/(3x(x-3)) = -1/(3x). Verified at x=1: -1/3. ASCII rendering is fully parenthesised, no second reading. x>0, x!=3 is needed for the cancellation, so the restriction is doing work.

SAM11-08.note: 2^(2x)*2^(3x+6)=2^15 -> 5x+6=15 -> x=9/5. Verified: 4^1.8*8^3.8 = 32768 = 32^3. STEM ECHO: option 3 equals the exponent in 32^3, but it is exactly the answer to 5x=15 (dropping the +6), a real error path. Agree with the author that it is not a usable elimination.

SAM11-09.note: xz = 3y^2+1 -> y = sqrt((xz-1)/3). Verified at x=2,y=1,z=2. y>0 selects the positive root, so the restriction is load-bearing. All four options are the four ways of misplacing the 1 and the 3 - clean distractor set.

SAM11-10.note: x-y=3, x^2+y^2=65 -> (7,4) or (-4,-7); 'positive' plus 'greater' selects 7. Distractor 4 is the lesser number, -4 the rejected root. Easy-medium; one of the softest items in the batch.

SAM11-11.note: Ratio of leading coefficients 6/2 = 3. 'As x increases without bound' is standard College Board phrasing and end behaviour of a rational function is in Advanced Math scope. Option 2.5 = 5/2 (wrong pair of coefficients), -6 a sign/coefficient slip. Medium.

SAM11-12.note: 2y^3=54 -> y=3 (x=6). Easiest item in the batch. Note 6 is offered as an option: it is x, the intermediate - the stem asks for y, so no ambiguity, but see self-report 2.

SAM11-13.note: Remainder theorem at the root of the divisor: p(1/2) = 0.5+2-1.5+5 = 6. Both conventions (divide by 2x-1 or by x-1/2) give the constant remainder 6, so no ambiguity. STEM ECHO: option 5 is the constant term - but that is the classic 'remainder = constant term' error, a legitimate distractor. 14 = p(1). The 1/2 root makes this a real module-2 hard item.

SAM11-14.note: 2x^3 - x^2 - 25x - 12; verified p(1) = -36 against the factored form. Distractors -1 and -12 are the OTHER coefficients of the same expansion - the best distractor set in the batch. Near-duplicate of SAM11-03. Borderline hard; I place it medium against the live scale.

SAM11-15.note: (8+2w)(10+2w)=168 -> w^2+9w-22=0 -> w=2 (12x14=168 checks). The 'border alone = 168' misreading gives w=3.39, not an option, so exclusivity holds. WEAK OPTION: 4 has no derivation I can find and coincides with 'four sides' in the stem; 12 is the framed width. Near-duplicate of SAM11-02 (geometric quadratic, reject a root).

SAM11-16.note: Vertex at x=5 lies OUTSIDE [0,3]; f decreasing there, so min at the endpoint x=3: -3. Distractor -7 = f(5), the unrestricted vertex value - this is the whole point of the item. STEM ECHO: 18 = f(0), also the constant term; legitimate (it is the max on the interval, the classic wrong endpoint). The second item where a restriction does real work, and correctly hard.

SAM11-17.note: R = 80p-2p^2, vertex p=20, R=800. Distractor 20 is the optimal PRICE (the intermediate), 1600 = 80*20. Same mechanism as SAM11-05.

SAM11-18.note: Zeros 3/2, -4, 3; sum 0.5. Distractors are the individual zeros (-4, 1.5) plus 2.5. Medium - the only trap is stopping at one zero.

SAM11-19.note: f(2)=f(6) puts the axis at x=4; 1 and 7 are symmetric about 4, so f(7)=f(1)=0 (explicitly: f(x) = -(x-4)^2+9). Genuinely hard and a good item. BUT the key equals a number printed in the stem (f(1)=0) - the author's stem-echo audit counted distractors only, so this was not counted, and it is the most consequential echo in the batch: a blind solver who either trusts or distrusts stem literals moves off chance on the KEY, not on a distractor.

SAM11-20.note: 16^(3/4)=8, x^8*(3/4)=x^6, y^(-3). Verified at x=1,y=2: value 1, matches 8/y^3 only. Distractors separate the 16^(3/4)=2 vs 8 error from the negative-exponent error - clean 2x2.

SAM11-21.note: 240/n - 240/(n+4) = 2 -> n^2+4n-480=0 -> n=20 (12 vs 10 dollars, checks). Distractor 24 = n+4, 12 and 10 the two shares - three of four options are real intermediate quantities, the strongest 'answer the wrong question' set in the batch. Hard.

SAM11-22.note: 3g(x)-4 = 6x^2+5 -> g = 2x^2+3; verified by substitution. Distractor 2x^2+9 comes from subtracting rather than adding the 4, 18x^2+19 from applying f in the wrong order. Medium.

SAM11-23.note: sqrt(x+7)=1+sqrt(x) -> 6=2sqrt(x) -> x=9; checks (4-3=1). No extraneous root to discard, which makes this easier than the usual radical item - the classic hard version has one. Medium.

SAM11-24.note: k^2-100>0 -> k>10 for positive k -> least integer 11. Distractor 10 gives a repeated root, i.e. NOT two distinct solutions - the strict-vs-nonstrict inequality is the whole item and the distractor is exactly right. 5 = sqrt(25), 100 = the discriminant boundary. Correctly hard.
